newsitem.title: USA: U.S. tests missile defense sensor.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tests missile defense sensor.

text.p: The U.S. military on Tuesday successfully tested a sensor designed to detect and track attacking nuclear missiles in a shot high over the Pacific Ocean, the Defense Department said.
The test was part of a multibillion dollar U.S. program that might one day provide a national missile defense for the United States.

The Pentagon said a rocket carrying an optical sensor and data system was fired from Kwajalein Missile Range in the Marshall Islands and the sensor located dummy warhead targets from a Minuteman-2 missile launched 21 minutes earlier from Vandenberg Air Force Base, California.

The sensor, built by Boeing Co., is in the initial test stage. It is designed to be mounted on small rockets that would be aimed to collide with enemy nuclear warheads once they are identified and tracked by the sensor.

"Initial indications are that the EKV (Exoatmospheric kill vehicle) successfully identified and tracked the simulated threat targets," the statement said, adding there was no attempt to actually destroy the dummy warheads.
The sensor is packaged to look out of the side of a rocket through an aluminum high-performance telescope.

The Clinton administration has scaled back former President Ronald Reagan's dream of developing a costly "Star Wars" umbrella defense of the whole United States against a massive nuclear missile attack.

But Republicans in Congress have pressed the Pentagon to expand its now-limited Ballistic Missile Defense Organization (BMDO) plan to protect only U.S. forces and bases from missile attack until a broader threat emerges after the Cold War.

The Defense Department has agreed to work to develop weapons for a national missile defense by 1999 and to make a decision then on whether to deploy it within three years after that if necessary to meet a realistic threat.
Meanwhile, Defense Secretary William Cohen has announced plans to spend an additional $2 billion on missile defense over the coming five years because of previous lags in spending and test problems.
Despite four test failures, the Pentagon said in April that experts had recommended the United States press ahead with work on a $17 billion component of its planned anti-missile defense.

The department said two independent study groups concluded that the design and concept were sound for an anti-missile missile built by Lockheed Martin Corp. for the so-called Theater High-Altitude Area Defense (THAAD).
The missile failed its fourth consecutive test on March 6, clouding the future of the THAAD program and baring the technical difficulties of a "Star Wars" defense launched by Reagan.
The missile, designed to smash into attacking nuclear or other missiles at altitudes of up to 50 miles (80 km), failed to hit a test target at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico.
